_comment: Safety batch A body translation · litellm (2026-11-06). Every URL was direct-fetched on 2026-11-06.

axes.model_access: This is one of its two main axes: the providers page records '100+ LLMs' behind one OpenAI-format API with bring-your-own keys, and self-hosted endpoints on the same page (Ollama, vLLM, Llamafile). Release notes record providers still being added (the 2026-11 entries include Microsoft 365 Copilot and Azure PTU capacity). No guardrail judgement is built in; it comes from external rails you attach.
axes.runtime: Self-hosting first: the simple-proxy page records pip install then `litellm --config config.yaml`, default port 4000. The deploy page records the ghcr.io/berriai/litellm image, a docker run example, Helm / Terraform, a Postgres dependency and the /health/readiness check. The site also records a hosted cloud usage path. Production requiring a database is stated plainly on the simple-proxy page.
axes.local_files: It reads your own config.yaml (model list, key references, guardrail settings); keys and routing definitions stay in your environment, and spend and logs go into the Postgres you manage. It does not read your application source tree - the file surface is configuration plus where you persist data.
axes.background: It is a long-running gateway process: queueing, retries and routing happen service-side, and surviving a shutdown depends on how you deploy it (Helm or a VM). The batch and asynchronous job surface (videos / batches) has only appeared in release notes; dedicated pages were not verified item by item and are recorded as unknown.
axes.tools: The MCP page records it acting as an 'MCP Gateway' offering 'governed access to tools': servers configured through config.yaml or the UI, transports HTTP / SSE / stdio, authentication via OAuth, API keys and AWS SigV4, with access scoped by key, team and organization. A2A, Auto Router, logging and OpenTelemetry pages sit in the documentation navigation.
axes.context: Context passes through from the caller; the gateway itself keeps no memory and does no compression. Virtual keys, budgets and teams are access-layer boundaries, not context-layer ones, and the effective window is whatever the routed model gives you.
axes.permissions: Access control is its core: the virtual-keys page records keys minted through /key/generate, model, budget, rate-limit and team scoping, a master key for administration, and scheduled rotation as an Enterprise capability. The guardrails page records that most integrations run in the open-source build while dynamic parameters and per-key rail control need Enterprise. Data flow follows whichever providers you attach. SSO and audit logs sit in the Enterprise framing (simple-proxy page). Compliance certifications and third-party audits were not found on official pages and are recorded as unknown.
axes.fit: Fits: teams collapsing many providers into one OpenAI-compatible entry point, governing spend and access per key or team, and insisting on self-hosting. Not a fit: anyone wanting only a thin client SDK, nor anyone for whom a vendor-backed hosted guardrail with compliance attestations is a requirement - rails here are external services you plug in, not a vendor guarantee.

sections.能力边界: What it governs is on record: model access, budgets and rate limits, team membership, which MCP tools a principal can see, and where external rails attach. What it does not claim: any training-use promise about content safety, or published numbers for how well anything blocks. Per-key rail control and dynamic parameters sit in the Enterprise framing, so the open-source / Enterprise split has to be checked line by line against the official pages.
sections.变更记录说明: Two official streams carry change history: the release_notes page inside the docs and the PyPI release record. Recorded on the verification day: release notes latest v1.108.0 (2026-11-04), PyPI latest 1.108.1 (2026-11-05). Recent entries also show security-relevant actions, such as the 2026-10-24 image-signing key change and trust-bundle adjustment, plus repeated spend-logging fixes - spend accuracy needs measurement, not a changelog headline.

runs:
This site has not completed measured runs; nothing here covers routing success rates, latency, guardrail block rates or accounting error.

**Suggested measurements** (three):

- Whether per-key spend accounting stays accurate for failed requests, batches and Bedrock inference profiles
- The real visibility of one MCP tool across key / team / organization layers
- Latency and blocking behaviour of pre_call versus post_call rails
unknowns:
- Hosted details and limits of batch / asynchronous jobs (videos, batches and similar)
- The full open-source versus Enterprise feature split (only the items the docs mention were verified)
- Data residency and retention terms of the official hosted cloud
- Compliance certifications and third-party audit reports
- Minimum deployment requirements beyond Helm / Terraform (bare-metal sizing, cache needs)
